title: Two small destroyers stand and fight

facts.text: On 1 December 1944 two small escort destroyers of the Imperial Japanese Navy, Kuwa and Take, left Manila guarding a supply convoy for the Japanese Army on Leyte. It was one of the runs Japan called the TA operations.
Kuwa's commanding officer, Yamashita Masamichi, 53, led the escort. Take had come through an air attack on the previous run on 25 November that killed 15 of her crew, including her navigator.
The convoy reached Ormoc Bay at 2330 on 2 December. Kuwa stood guard while Take moved close inshore to pick up survivors of an earlier convoy, and the transports began ferrying supplies ashore.

Three new American destroyers of Destroyer Division 120, Allen M. Sumner, Moale and Cooper, under Commander John C. Zahm, slipped into the bay and opened fire at 0008 on 3 December. The Japanese had been watching the sky for aircraft.
Yamashita did not run. Kuwa charged the three larger ships and fired her torpedoes, but within minutes she was a burning wreck. Yamashita was killed and about half her crew died with her.
Take swung round to bring her weapons to bear and raced into the shallows at 24 knots. Her crew fired two of her last three torpedoes by hand.

At about 0013 a torpedo hit Cooper. She broke in two and sank within a minute. Which Japanese ship fired it is still unsettled: the U.S. Navy's official chronology says possibly Kuwa, and the Japanese records do not decide between Kuwa and Take.
Cooper lost 191 men. Japanese forces nearby kept rescue ships away, and 168 survivors were picked up by Black Cat PBY flying boats.
Two minutes after Cooper went down, a 5 inch shell hit Take's forward engine room and failed to explode. The flooding still forced her crew out of it, and she lost her port shaft.
The two surviving American destroyers were ordered out of the bay. At 0330 the Japanese left too, and a landing ship paused to pull eight of Kuwa's men from the water.
At 0940 Take radioed: "Attacked by three enemy ships. Sank one and drove the others off to the south." She limped back to Manila on one shaft on 4 December.
Take survived the war. She surrendered at Maizuru in August 1945, carried Japanese troops home from overseas, and in July 1947 was handed to Britain as war reparations and scrapped.

declassified.fact: The Black Cat rescue planes worked through the night and into the next day. One PBY flying boat carried 56 of Cooper's survivors on top of its own crew of eight.
